```

-> Select the news to read (e.g. 1 3 5), select 0 to read them all or press "enter" to proceed with update: 3

---
Title: Mkinitcpio >=42 requires manual intervention for TPM2-based unlocking of LUKS devices
Author: David Runge
Publication date: 2026-09-22
URL: https://www.archlinux.org/news/mkinitcpio-42-requires-manual-intervention-for-tpm2-based-unlocking-of-luks-devices/
---

Starting with package version 42-1, the mkinitcpio systemd hook now includes systemd-pcrosseparator.service (as intended by systemd v261).
This affects the measurements of PCR values 0-7, 9 and 12-14.
If you configured the systemd hook and unlock LUKS partitions, that depend on these values, you need to re-enroll the TPM2 in use.
For guidance, please refer to systemd-cryptenroll(1), or the ArchWiki article on systemd-cryptenroll, when using pinned values.
Refer to systemd-pcrlock(8), when relying on custom policies and a disabled systemd-pcrlock-make-policy.service.

==> Press "enter" to continue 

```

Short answer: probably not, but it's worth a 30-second check, because the news item only affects one specific setup.

**Who is affected:** people whose LUKS volume is unlocked automatically by the **TPM2 chip** (enrolled with `systemd-cryptenroll`), *and* whose initramfs uses the **systemd hook**. If that's you, the update changes the PCR measurements, so the TPM would no longer release the key and you'd be asked for a passphrase (or locked out if you have no passphrase).

**Who is not affected:** a standard LUKS install where you type a passphrase at boot (or use a keyfile) doesn't depend on any of this. CachyOS doesn't set up TPM2 unlocking by default, so if you just chose "encrypt disk" in the installer and enter your password at boot, you're almost certainly fine.

**Quick check before you reboot:**

```
sudo systemd-cryptenroll /dev/YOUR_LUKS_PARTITION
```

(Find the partition with `lsblk -f`; it's the one with type `crypto_LUKS`.) If the output lists only `password` slots, you're not using TPM2 and can ignore the news item. If it shows a `tpm2` slot, you're affected.

Also confirm which hook you use:

```
grep ^HOOKS /etc/mkinitcpio.conf /etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d/* 2>/dev/null
```

If it shows `udev` rather than `systemd`, the news item doesn't apply to you either.

**If you do have a TPM2 slot**, after the update, and before relying on auto-unlock, re-enroll:

```
sudo systemd-cryptenroll --wipe-slot=tpm2 --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=7 /dev/YOUR_LUKS_PARTITION
```

(Adjust the PCR list to whatever you originally used.) Make sure you still have a working passphrase slot as a fallback first.

**The other news items are worth acting on too**, since they're security fixes rather than manual interventions: the PHP one (only if you have PHP installed) and the `ca-certificates-mozilla` one will just be pulled in by the normal upgrade. Item 5, the AUR malicious packages incident, is worth reading (press `5` on the next prompt) if you use AUR helpers, to check whether any package you have installed is on the list.

So: run the `cryptenroll` check, and if it shows only a password slot, press enter and proceed.

~
❯ sudo systemd-cryptenroll /dev/YOUR_LUKS_PARTITION
[sudo] password for mll:
Device /dev/YOUR_LUKS_PARTITION does not exist or access denied.
Failed to allocate libcryptsetup context: Block device required

~ 8s
❯ grep ^HOOKS /etc/mkinitcpio.conf /etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d/* 2>/dev/null
/etc/mkinitcpio.conf:HOOKS=(base systemd autodetect microcode kms modconf block keyboard sd-vconsole plymouth sd-encrypt filesystems)
/etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d/10-chwd-kms.conf:HOOKS=(${HOOKS[@]/kms/})
/etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d/10-limine-snapper-sync.conf:HOOKS+=(sd-btrfs-overlayfs)

~
❯

Two things here. First, `/dev/YOUR_LUKS_PARTITION` was a placeholder, so I should have been clearer that you need to substitute your real device. Second, your hooks output matters: you use the **systemd** hook with **sd-encrypt**, so the news item *could* apply if you have a TPM2 slot. That's why the check is worth finishing.

Find your actual LUKS partition:

```
lsblk -f
```

Look for the row with `crypto_LUKS` in the FSTYPE column (probably something like `/dev/nvme0n1p2` or `/dev/sda2`). Then run the check with that path:

```
sudo systemd-cryptenroll /dev/nvme0n1p2
```

(Replace with your real device.)

How to read the result:

- **Only `password` slots listed:** you're not using TPM2 unlocking. Ignore the news item and proceed with the update.
- **A `tpm2` slot listed:** you're affected. Make sure you know your LUKS passphrase (the fallback), do the update, and if the next boot asks for the passphrase instead of auto-unlocking, enter it and re-enroll with:

```
sudo systemd-cryptenroll --wipe-slot=tpm2 --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=7 /dev/nvme0n1p2
```

Use whatever PCR list you originally enrolled with if it wasn't just 7.

Since you said you've been unlocking with your normal install setup and CachyOS doesn't enable TPM2 by default, I expect you'll see only password slots. But run the check before rebooting, since it takes a few seconds and removes the doubt.

❯ lsblk -f
NAME         FSTYPE FSVER LABEL      UUID                                 FSAVAIL FSUSE% MOUNTPOINTS
sda
|-sda1       exfat  1.0   LINUX-BEST 8402-1A96
`-sda2       vfat   FAT16 VTOYEFI    1998-3510
zram0        swap   1     zram0      [an id, kept out]                [SWAP]
nvme0n1
|-nvme0n1p1  vfat   FAT32            1B50-DB66                               1.7G    58% /boot
`-nvme0n1p2  crypto 2                [an id, kept out]
  `-luks-[an id, kept out]
             btrfs                   [an id, kept out]  253.9G    73% /var/tmp
                                                                                         /var/log
                                                                                         /var/cache
                                                                                         /home
                                                                                         /srv
                                                                                         /root
                                                                                         /

~
❯ sudo systemd-cryptenroll /dev/nvme0n1p2
SLOT TYPE

~
❯

You're clear. The output shows only slot 0 with type `password`, so there's no TPM2 slot. Your LUKS volume is unlocked by typing your passphrase at boot, and the mkinitcpio 42 change (the `systemd-pcrosseparator.service` addition) only affects TPM2-bound unlocking. Nothing to re-enroll, nothing to do.

Go ahead and press enter to continue the update.

Two small things to keep in mind:

- **Reboot afterward** so the new initramfs, kernel, and `ca-certificates-mozilla` update take effect. You'll enter your passphrase as usual.
- **Item 5 (the AUR malicious packages incident)** is worth a quick read if you have any AUR packages installed. You can press `5` at the news prompt before proceeding, or check the news page afterward. It's about whether any packages you installed from the AUR are on the affected list, which is independent of your disk encryption.

The PHP fix only matters if you have PHP installed, and it comes in with the normal upgrade either way.

what is tpm bound unlocking ? my motherboard has tpm, so im not using it and it actually easy to decrypt the drive on any other device as it is not bound to tpm, i can just install it into any other pc enter the password and it will work ?

TPM-bound unlocking means the LUKS key is stored (sealed) inside the TPM chip instead of you typing it. At boot, the TPM checks that the machine is in a trusted state (firmware, bootloader, Secure Boot settings, etc., measured into registers called PCRs) and only then releases the key. You get automatic unlock with no password prompt, and the drive can't be unlocked on another machine because the key lives in *this* motherboard's chip.

**Your understanding of your own setup is correct.** Your LUKS volume is protected only by your passphrase, so you can move the NVMe drive to any other PC, boot a live USB, run `cryptsetup open /dev/nvme0n1p2` and enter the passphrase, and it works. That's actually a feature: if your motherboard dies, your data isn't stranded.

**The tradeoffs:**

| | Passphrase only (you) | TPM-bound |
|---|---|---|
| Convenience | Type password every boot | Automatic unlock |
| Drive moved to another PC | Works with passphrase | Can't unlock via TPM; needs the passphrase/recovery key fallback |
| Motherboard failure | No problem | Need the fallback passphrase |
| Security | Entirely depends on passphrase strength | Protects against theft of just the drive, but weak if no PIN is set |

**A caveat about TPM-only unlocking:** if the TPM releases the key automatically with no PIN, anyone who steals the *whole laptop/PC* gets as far as your login screen, so your security shifts to your user password and OS vulnerabilities. Many people add a TPM PIN (`--tpm2-with-pin=yes`) to get the best of both.

For your setup, a strong passphrase is a perfectly solid choice. TPM unlocking mainly buys convenience, and in your case it would also add the exact maintenance burden that news item described (re-enrolling after boot-chain changes).
what are the most beautiful modern kde themes, where to see them, and do they have github ? and is there are glossy, and fancy looking ones ? research the subject

Yes, there are glossy, glass-style KDE themes, and nearly all of them are on GitHub. Browsing and installing them is easy, but the fancy glass effects need some care on a rolling distro like CachyOS.

## Where to browse

- **KDE Store (store.kde.org):** Every theme has screenshots, ratings and comments, and most link to their GitHub source.
- **System Settings:** Go to Appearance → Colors & Themes → Global Themes → Get New. This installs from the same store.
- **GitHub:** Themes with several parts (Plasma style, window decorations, Kvantum, icons) are usually easier to install from the repo's `install.sh`.

## Beautiful modern themes (all on GitHub)

- **WhiteSur-kde** (`vinceliuice/WhiteSur-kde`): A macOS Big Sur-style theme. The repo bundles an Aurorae window theme, a Kvantum theme, a color scheme, a Plasma desktop theme and a global theme, and recommends the Kvantum engine for the best look. It also has a WhiteSurLiquid variant with glass-like translucency inspired by macOS Liquid Glass.
- **Layan, Sweet, Nordic, Materia, Orchis, Fluent:** These are long-standing popular picks. Layan comes in light and dark variants, and Fluent gives a Windows 11 look. Sweet and Nordic are by EliverLara, and Layan, WhiteSur and Orchis are by vinceliuice. That list comes from an older roundup, so check each theme's repo for Plasma 6 support and recent commits.
- **Catppuccin** (`catppuccin/kde`): Pastel palettes if you prefer flat and cozy over glossy. I'm recalling this one from memory rather than from my searches.

## Glossy and fancy options

- **Liquid Glass setups.** `david-x3d/kde-plasma-liquid-glass-theme` is a macOS Tahoe-inspired setup. It combines a transparent Layan, Darkly, BreezeEnhanced, WhiteSur icons, Better Blur DX and KDE Rounded Corners. It's a curated bundle with an installer, not an official theme.
- **kwin-effects-glass** (`4v3ngR/kwin-effects-glass`): A fork of the Plasma 6 blur effect with extra features and bug fixes, plus an improved refraction shader. The author also publishes theme patches and an application/window theme styled to match. Arch users can get it with `yay -S kwin-effects-glass-git`. One distro build of it requires KWin 6.6 or newer.
- **Better Blur DX:** A KWin effect that adds force blur, adjustable parameters, corner radius and refraction, which bends the background behind blurred windows like a lens.
- **L4ki's Blur-Glassy and Wings:** Blur-Glassy is a very transparent, blurred light global theme with matching Kvantum, window decoration and splash screen parts. Its source is `github.com/L4ki/Blur-Glassy`. The same author's Wings Light theme is rounded, transparent and blurred, with blurred widgets.

## Things to watch on CachyOS

1. **Rebuild after KWin updates.** The Better Blur DX effect has to be rebuilt for each KWin version because of binary compatibility. The glass plugins likely work the same way. On Arch, a KWin update can break them until the AUR package catches up, so check the plugin's issues page before a big upgrade.
2. **Vet AUR packages.** You just saw the "Active AUR malicious packages incident" news item, so it's worth skimming the PKGBUILD and checking the maintainer before installing `-git` packages like `kwin-effects-glass-git`.
3. **Expect some visual bugs.** In the KDE Store comments, some WhiteSur users report a translucent square border around windows or thick borders. The usual fixes involve Kvantum settings, compositor settings or window decoration variants.
4. **Back up first.** The Liquid Glass repo itself warns that Plasma theme internals can change between KDE versions, and recommends backing up your current settings. Plasma 6.6 also helps here: you can now save your current look as a new global theme from System Settings.

If you want the glossiest result, install WhiteSur or Layan first, then add a glass blur effect. Skip the all-in-one Liquid Glass bundle until you know the individual parts work on your setup. If you tell me whether you prefer a macOS, Windows 11 or something-else look, I can narrow this down.
is there any theme that has at least 100 stars on github and not some unstable shit like most of them are ?

Yes. Two themes I confirmed clear 100 stars easily, and a few others are well packaged, though I couldn't verify their star counts. Stars measure popularity, not stability, and the flaky parts of KDE theming are mostly not the themes themselves.

## Confirmed over 100 stars

- **WhiteSur-kde** (`vinceliuice/WhiteSur-kde`): About 1.3k stars. It's a macOS-style theme. The repo includes a variant called WhiteSurLiquid, with glass-like translucency inspired by macOS Liquid Glass. This is your best bet for glossy.
- **Layan-kde** (`vinceliuice/Layan-kde`): 536 stars. It's a flat design theme with Aurorae window themes, Kvantum themes, color schemes, Plasma desktop themes and look-and-feel themes. This is the less flashy, more conservative option.

## Likely solid, but I couldn't verify their star counts

- **Klassy** (`paulmcauley/klassy`): A highly customizable window decoration, application style and global theme plugin, with a preset called "Glassy Klassy". Its packaged versions track Plasma releases (6.4 and 6.5.x showed up in packaging), which is a good sign for stability.
- **Darkly** (`Bali10050/Darkly`): A Qt application style forked from Lightly, with an AUR package last updated in March 2026. It's also packaged for Gentoo, openSUSE and Solus.
- **Catppuccin** (`catppuccin/kde`): A color scheme and window decoration set, not a full restyle. Its AUR package was updated in August 2026. Since it's mostly color files, there's very little to break.

I couldn't pull the star count for these three, so check the repo pages for that.

## Where the instability comes from

1. **Compiled KWin plugins break on updates.** Better Blur DX has to be rebuilt for each KWin version. The glass effects work the same way, so a rolling distro like CachyOS can break them after a KWin update. Stick to data-only themes if stability matters most.
2. **Data-only themes are the safest.** Plasma style, Kvantum, Aurorae and color schemes are just files, so they rarely break on update. WhiteSur and Layan are mostly that.
3. **Some WhiteSur bugs exist.** Users report a translucent square border around windows and thick borders even with "No Borders" set, some with Nvidia and display scaling. Layan users in the same comments reported not having those problems. I couldn't confirm how recently Layan has been updated, so check its commit history.

## What I'd do

For a stable setup that still looks good, install Layan or WhiteSur with the Kvantum theme and matching icons, and skip the glass plugins. If it breaks, you can switch themes in System Settings without rebuilding anything. Try the glass blur effect later, once the base is working.

why do they all look like a garbage mess ? isnt kde has the most canonical way of theming the fucking kde ? isnt there any editor ? why there is a mess of scripts on top of fucking scripts that mess with the whole fucking system without any reliable rollback ?

Your frustration is fair, and the mess has a structural cause.

## Why it's a mess

KDE does have a canonical theming system, but it's split into many separate layers. Colors, icons and cursors are simple files. The Plasma style (panel, menus) is SVG. Window decorations are either Aurorae themes or compiled C++ plugins. The widget style that draws buttons and scrollbars (Breeze, Darkly, Klassy) is compiled C++ code, or Kvantum's SVG engine. Blur and glass effects are KWin plugins. GTK apps are themed separately and don't follow any of it automatically.

A **Global Theme** is just a bundle that points at all of these. It doesn't unify them or guarantee they look good together. So a hobbyist who wants a cohesive look has to combine several layers by hand, and when it doesn't fit, they write an `install.sh` that copies files around. Most of the garbage you see comes from half-matching layers, like a transparent Plasma style with an opaque Kvantum theme.

## Is there an editor?

There's no single one, but there are partial ones:

- **System Settings → Colors:** lets you edit and save your own color scheme.
- **Kvantum Manager:** configures Kvantum themes.
- **Klassy Settings:** one app for window decoration and application style settings, with presets such as "Glassy Klassy". It's the closest thing to a real theme editor.
- **Plasma 6.6 and later:** you can save your current appearance (colors, window decoration, icons and so on) as a new global theme. That's also a basic restore point for the appearance layers, though it doesn't cover compiled plugins or KWin effects.

For Plasma style SVGs there's no GUI at all. People edit them by hand in Inkscape.

## Why there's no reliable rollback

Nobody owns the whole stack. Install scripts write to `~/.local/share`, `~/.config` and sometimes `/usr`, and they track nothing. The KDE Store route through System Settings is the exception: the theme can be uninstalled from the same window, as long as it only contains data files.

## What I'd do

1. **Prefer the in-app "Get New" route** for data-only themes.
2. **Skim any `install.sh` before running it:** `grep -nE "sudo|/usr|/etc|rm -" install.sh`. If it only touches `~/.local` and `~/.config`, the damage is limited.
3. **Back up before experimenting:** `cp -a ~/.config ~/config-backup`. Also copy `~/.local/share/{plasma,aurorae,color-schemes,icons}` if you'll install themes there. To restore, log out and copy them back from a TTY.
4. **Stay with Breeze:** it's the one theme KDE itself maintains. Plasma 6.5 added fully rounded window corners and automatic light/dark switching. Change the accent color, wallpaper and icon theme and you get a clean look with nothing to break.

Your `/home` is on btrfs, so you can also snapshot it before experimenting, which is a far better rollback than copying folders. If you show me `sudo btrfs subvolume list /`, I can give you the exact commands.
how do i snapshot it in a proper way in cachyos ? im on btrfs

On CachyOS the proper tool is **Snapper**, and from your mkinitcpio hooks (`limine-snapper-sync`) it's already set up for the root filesystem. There's a catch for what you want to do.

## The catch: `/home` is separate

CachyOS uses an `@` / `@home` subvolume layout, and `@home` is its own subvolume, so it isn't part of an `@` snapshot. Your theme experiments change files in `~/.config` and `~/.local/share`, so a root snapshot won't protect them. You need a Snapper config for `/home`. You can add one in Btrfs Assistant.

## 1. Check what exists

```
sudo snapper list-configs
```

If you only see `root`, there's no home config yet.

## 2. Create a home config (once)

```
sudo snapper -c home create-config /home
```

Optionally stop it from taking automatic hourly snapshots, so you only get the ones you take:

```
sudo snapper -c home set-config TIMELINE_CREATE=no
```

## 3. Snapshot before experimenting

```
sudo snapper -c home create --cleanup-algorithm number -d "before theming"
```

This is instant, and it costs almost no space until files change. The `number` cleanup lets Snapper prune it automatically later.

## 4. If the experiment goes wrong

First see what changed:

```
sudo snapper -c home list
sudo snapper -c home status N..0 | grep -E "\.config/|\.local/share/"
```

(`N` is the snapshot number, `0` is the current state.) Then revert just the theme-related folders:

```
sudo snapper -c home undochange N..0 /home/mll/.config /home/mll/.local/share/plasma
```

Do this from a TTY or after logging out of Plasma, so KDE doesn't rewrite its config while you restore. Be selective with `undochange`, because it also reverts any other file changes in those paths since the snapshot. You can also browse a snapshot at `/home/.snapshots/N/snapshot/` and copy single files back.

## 5. Clean up

```
sudo snapper -c home delete N
```

## Rolling back the system itself

This doesn't cover system files like `/usr` or the initramfs. Those are what the root config protects. CachyOS pairs Snapper with the Limine bootloader through `limine-snapper-sync`, so you can pick a snapshot from the Limine boot menu. If you want a GUI, `btrfs-assistant-launcher` also has a Snapper tab.

## Things to watch

- **Boot partition space:** your `/boot` was at 58% in `lsblk`. `limine-snapper-sync` stops adding snapshot entries when the ESP usage limit of 85% is exceeded. You're fine now, but don't let snapshots pile up.
- **Snapshots aren't backups.** They live on the same disk, so if the NVMe dies, they go with it.

For the theme work, take a root snapshot and a home snapshot before installing anything, then experiment freely.
What is the best de, stack to build most robust wery customized look/de on linux without shit and sticks like it is on kde mr gnome ?

There's no setup where customization is free of glue. The choice is between messy scripts you don't control and a small set of parts you can read and version. The most robust version of that is a Wayland compositor with a Quickshell-based shell.

## The stack

1. **Compositor (window manager):**
   - **Niri**: scrollable tiling, small, simple config. I'd pick it for robustness.
   - **Hyprland**: the most eye candy (blur, animations), but it changes faster and breaks more often.
   - **Sway**: the most conservative, but plain-looking.

   This is from general knowledge, not my searches, so check each project's release notes.
2. **Shell (bar, launcher, notifications, lock screen, OSD):** **Quickshell**, a Qt/QML toolkit where you write the shell yourself. You can also use a ready-made one built on it:
   - **Noctalia**: supports Niri, Hyprland, Sway, Scroll, Labwc and MangoWC, generates colors from your wallpaper, and has 30+ plugins.
   - **Caelestia**: a Quickshell/QML shell with fluid animations, designed for Hyprland.
3. **Glue you still need:** an xdg portal for screen sharing and file dialogs, a polkit agent, a display manager, and Kvantum or qt6ct plus GTK settings for app theming.

## Caveats

- **It's a shell, not a full DE.** Noctalia says it's not a full desktop environment and doesn't handle the login greeter or drive mounting. You'll configure those separately.
- **These projects move fast.** Noctalia shipped ten releases between early March and early April 2026. That means active development, but also churn.
- **Avoid script-pile dotfile packs.** HyDE and ML4W are install-and-update-script configurations, which is the same pattern you're complaining about.
- **Your apps are still GTK and Qt.** Theming them stays the hard part, as in KDE. Wallpaper-derived colors reduce the work, but won't remove it.

## Making it robust

Keep your config in git, or use home-manager, which works on CachyOS without NixOS. Combined with the Btrfs snapshots from earlier, you get real rollback: `git revert`, or restore a snapshot.

If you'd rather not leave KDE, the minimal path from earlier (Breeze plus accent color, or Klassy) is the least fragile.

What about dwm ? Is there dwm in rust ?

dwm is C, X11-only, and configured by editing `config.h` and recompiling. There's no Rust dwm clone, but there are Rust window managers in the same spirit.

## Rust options

- **LeftWM** (X11): a tiling window manager written in Rust for stability and performance, built around theming. It's the closest to dwm in being X11-only, but it uses runtime config and themes instead of recompiling.
- **Pinnacle** (Wayland): a Wayland compositor built in Rust using Smithay, with a tiling window manager at its core in the style of i3 and sway. You configure it in Lua or Rust. Smithay is also the Rust library for writing your own compositor.
- **Niri** (Wayland): Rust too, from my own knowledge rather than these searches. It's the one I'd pick for robustness.
- **Penrose**: a Rust library for building your own window manager, which is the dwm philosophy in a different language. Again from my own knowledge, so check its repo for current state.

## The Wayland dwm

**dwl** is the real dwm equivalent: a compact, hackable wlroots compositor intended to fill the same space on Wayland that dwm does on X11. It's written in C and patched or recompiled like dwm. For blur and rounded corners, there's a wlroots base called scenefx described as "dwm but wayland".

## Caveats

- **Patches are fragile.** dwm's customization model is patches, and they conflict when stacked. That's the "scripts on scripts" problem again, just in C.
- **No eye candy by default.** dwm has no blur, shadows or animations. On X11 you'd add picom.
- **A bare WM isn't a DE.** You still build the bar, launcher, notifications and lock screen yourself, or use something like Noctalia on top of Niri.

If you want minimal and robust, use Niri. If you want to write the compositor logic in code, use Pinnacle or Penrose. If you want the real dwm experience, use dwm or dwl.
is there one click snapshot of the whole system tui or gui ?

Yes, on CachyOS that's **Btrfs Assistant**, a GUI for Snapper.

```
btrfs-assistant-launcher
```

The CachyOS wiki recommends it for people who prefer a GUI for managing Btrfs and snapshots. It also covers automatic cleanup and deleting snapshots, and suggests installing `btrfsmaintenance` first. In its Snapper tab you can pick a config (`root` or `home`) and create or delete snapshots. I haven't verified the exact button layout, so check it on your screen.

## No TUI

I didn't find a dedicated snapper TUI. One CachyOS forum thread asks for a keyboard-driven restore tool, which suggests there isn't one. In that thread, a commenter notes that with Limine and `limine-snapper-sync` you get a snapshot picker at boot. You already have that set up, so it works as your restore menu.

## One command for "the whole system"

Snapper treats root and home separately, so "whole system" means one snapshot per config. A shell alias in `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc` covers both:

```
alias snapall='sudo snapper -c root create --cleanup-algorithm number -d "manual" && sudo snapper -c home create --cleanup-algorithm number -d "manual"'
```

This assumes you created the `home` config from my earlier steps. Then `snapall` takes both snapshots in about a second. You could also use the same two commands in a small script bound to a hotkey or launcher.

## What a snapshot doesn't cover

Your `/boot` is a separate FAT partition, and Btrfs snapshots don't include it, so it isn't covered. That's why booting a snapshot from the Limine menu is the safer restore path, and why you should avoid hand-copying files back into a live root.
dont assume anything, i want solid zero to hero all in one solution

Here's the full setup, with a verification step first. CachyOS already ships most of it, and your hooks suggest the Limine part is installed.

## 0. Check what you actually have

```
sudo snapper list-configs
sudo btrfs subvolume show /home
pacman -Q snapper snap-pac btrfs-assistant btrfsmaintenance limine-snapper-sync
systemctl list-unit-files | grep -Ei 'snapper|limine'
df -h /boot
```

You want:
- A `root` config listed.
- `/home` showing as its own subvolume.
- All five packages present.

Install any missing package from the CachyOS repos with `sudo pacman -S <name>`. If `/home` isn't a subvolume, stop and tell me, because the home steps won't work.

`snap-pac` ships with CachyOS by default, so every pacman install, upgrade or removal already gets automatic before/after root snapshots. The default config only covers root, and other subvolumes like `/home` need their own config.

## 1. Set a sane retention for root

The CachyOS wiki recommends keeping about 10 snapshots, with timeline snapshots off and number-based cleanup on.

```
sudo snapper -c root set-config TIMELINE_CREATE=no NUMBER_CLEANUP=yes NUMBER_LIMIT=10 NUMBER_LIMIT_IMPORTANT=10 NUMBER_MIN_AGE=3600
sudo systemctl enable --now snapper-cleanup.timer
```

## 2. Add a config for /home

```
sudo snapper -c home create-config /home
sudo snapper -c home set-config TIMELINE_CREATE=no NUMBER_CLEANUP=yes NUMBER_LIMIT=5 NUMBER_LIMIT_IMPORTANT=5 NUMBER_MIN_AGE=3600
```

I set the limit lower because home snapshots hold onto deleted large files (games, caches), so they eat space. Check with `sudo btrfs filesystem usage /` occasionally.

## 3. Limit boot-menu entries

In `/etc/limine-snapper-sync.conf`, `MAX_SNAPSHOT_ENTRIES` caps how many snapshots show in the Limine menu, and the right number depends on your FAT32 boot partition size. The wiki suggests 10. Back up the file first with `sudo cp /etc/limine-snapper-sync.conf{,.orig}`, then edit it. After snapshot changes, regenerate the entries with `sudo limine-mkinitcpio`.

## 4. One-click snapshot of everything

```
sudo tee /usr/local/bin/snapall >/dev/null <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
[ "$EUID" -eq 0 ] || exec sudo "$0" "$@"
desc="${*:-manual snapshot}"
for cfg in root home; do
  if snapper -c "$cfg" get-config >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    snapper -c "$cfg" create --type single --cleanup-algorithm number --description "$desc" && echo "ok: $cfg"
  else
    echo "skipped (no config): $cfg"
  fi
done
EOF
sudo chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/snapall
```

Run `snapall "before theming"` from any terminal. For a clickable launcher:

```
cat > ~/.local/share/applications/snapall.desktop <<'EOF'
[Desktop Entry]
Type=Application
Name=Snapshot Everything
Exec=/usr/local/bin/snapall "from launcher"
Terminal=true
Icon=camera-photo
EOF
```

The GUI equivalent is `btrfs-assistant-launcher`, then the Snapper tab.

## 5. Test it once before you rely on it

```
echo hello > ~/snaptest.txt
snapall "test"
rm ~/snaptest.txt
sudo snapper -c home list
```

Take the snapshot number `N` from that list and copy the file back with `cp /home/.snapshots/N/snapshot/$USER/snaptest.txt ~/`. Then reboot once and confirm snapshots appear in the Limine menu.

## 6. Restoring

- **A file or folder in /home:** copy it from `/home/.snapshots/N/snapshot/...`, or use `sudo snapper -c home undochange N..0 <path>` after logging out.
- **The whole system:** pick a snapshot and kernel in the Limine menu, boot it (read-only), click "Restore now" in the popup, answer the prompts, then reboot.
- **Limit:** if the snapshot you want involved a kernel update, you can't roll back to it.

## 7. What snapshots don't protect

The wiki says snapshots don't help with bootloader problems or hardware failure, and aren't a replacement for backups, because they live on the same disk. Since you're on LUKS, I'd also make a header backup now, because a damaged header makes your data unrecoverable:

```
sudo cryptsetup luksHeaderBackup /dev/nvme0n1p2 --header-backup-file ~/luks-header.img
sudo tar czf ~/esp-backup.tar.gz -C /boot .
```

Copy both files to an external drive and delete the local copies. Anyone with the header file plus your old passphrase can unlock the volume, so keep it somewhere safe.

For real backups, I'd use `restic` or `btrfs send` to an external disk. I can write that setup next if you want.

## Your language questions

- **Is Nushell written in Rust?** Yes. It's a good interactive shell and works well for structured-data scripts. For a root-level tool shipped to many distros, it's a poor choice. Every user would need Nushell installed, and as far as I know it's still pre-1.0, so scripts can break between versions. It's not better than Python for complex programs, just better for pipelines.
- **Python:** ubiquitous and quick to write, but every distro package then depends on a specific interpreter and libraries. Completion support is also weakest for Nushell.
- **F# with NativeAOT:** it works, but cross-distro packaging is painful. NativeAOT builds per target and libc, and distro build farms dislike NuGet restores. The TUI ecosystem is also much smaller. This is from my own knowledge, so verify it before committing.
- **Rust:** a static musl binary per architecture works on every distro. `ratatui` covers the TUI, and `cargo-deb` / `cargo-generate-rpm` / a PKGBUILD cover packaging.

## Design

- Build a core library, a CLI, and a ratatui TUI as thin layers over it. Run `snapper` and parse its machine-readable output (`--jsonout` or `--csvout`, check your version), not the human tables.
- Define a backend trait. `snap-pac` and `limine-snapper-sync` are Arch and CachyOS specific, while other distros use different hooks and boot-menu integrations. I haven't verified each one, so don't claim "all distros" until you've tested them. Start with Arch/CachyOS, then openSUSE, Fedora and Debian/Ubuntu, one at a time. Limit the scope to Btrfs and snapper-backed setups.
- **Don't auto-install packages from the tool itself.** Declare `snapper` etc. as package dependencies, so the package manager handles them. Add a `snapall doctor` / `snapall setup` command for tarball installs that detects the distro, shows what it would install, and asks first.

## Completions

`clap_complete_nushell` generates Nushell completions for clap-based CLIs. Its output is a module of `export extern` signatures, with value completers for fixed choices. It's now maintained as part of clap. Generate completions at build time for Nushell, fish, bash and zsh, and ship them in the package. Also add a `snapall completions <shell>` subcommand for manual installs, like juliaup does with its completion generator.

Installed paths I believe are right, but verify: `/usr/share/bash-completion/completions/snapall`, `/usr/share/fish/vendor_completions.d/snapall.fish`, `/usr/share/zsh/site-functions/_snapall`, and `/usr/share/nushell/vendor/autoload/snapall.nu` (check `$nu.vendor-autoload-dirs`). Dynamic values like snapshot numbers need a custom completer, such as a hidden `snapall __complete` command.

## argenv

Make it the single source of truth for the argv and env contract, then generate completions, man page and `--help` from it. The risk is that your tool's quality depends on argenv being mature. Test the generated completions in CI so a contract change can't silently break them.

## CI and packaging

On a version tag, a GitHub Actions matrix would:

1. Build musl binaries for x86_64 and aarch64.
2. Produce `.deb`, `.rpm` and a PKGBUILD for the AUR.
3. Publish to GitHub Releases.
4. Push to COPR (Fedora) and the openSUSE Build Service, which can build deb, rpm and Arch packages from one source (verify).

For tests, containers can't run Btrfs snapshots. Use a loopback Btrfs image on a runner with root access, or a VM, and run snapper against it.

what license forces users to contribute upstream ?

No license can force anyone to send their changes back to *you*. The closest thing is **copyleft**, which forces them to share their changes with whoever receives their version. That's reciprocity, not a patch pipeline to the original project.

| License | What it makes people do |
|---|---|
| **GPL-3.0** | If you distribute a modified or derived version, you must give recipients the source under the GPL. If you only use it privately, you owe nothing. |
| **AGPL-3.0** | The same, plus users who interact with a modified version over a network must be offered the source. The strongest mainstream option, but the network clause barely matters for a CLI tool like snapall. |
| **MPL-2.0** | File-level copyleft: changes to MPL-licensed files must be shared. Everything else in the larger work can stay proprietary. |
| **LGPL** | Copyleft for the library itself, with linking allowed from proprietary code. |

With all of these, the obligation is to share source with the people they distribute to. A fork can stay a fork forever, and nobody has to open a pull request. A few niche licenses (Artistic 1.0, the old Qt license) lean toward "offer it back to the author", but they still aren't mandatory. They're poorly accepted by distros, and I'm not certain of their exact terms, so read the text before considering one.

**Choosing a license for snapall:**
- **Packaging:** Debian, Fedora, Arch and nixpkgs all package GPL and AGPL software without trouble.
- **Dependencies:** MIT and Apache-2.0 dependencies are compatible with GPL-3.0 and AGPL-3.0. That includes argenv. Apache-2.0 is not compatible with GPL-2.0-only.
- **snapper itself:** snapall only runs snapper as a separate program and never links it, so snapper's own license doesn't constrain snapall's.
- **Trade-off:** copyleft keeps forks open, but it makes some companies avoid the project, and it won't get you more contributions. Contributions come from making it easy: good issues, a clear `CONTRIBUTING.md`, and fast reviews.
- **Changing it now is easy:** you hold all the copyright today. Once other people contribute, relicensing needs their consent, unless you collect a CLA beforehand.

can people and companies have their private fork without sharing it by default and only sharing when they want to or dont share at all ?

Yes to all three. The GPL's duties start only when someone **conveys** a copy to another party. Using or modifying the software creates no duty at all.

- **Private fork:** you or a company can modify it and run it forever without sharing it with anyone, including upstream.
- **Inside one company:** employees, and contractors working on the company's behalf, don't count as "someone else". A separate legal entity does: a subsidiary, a customer or a partner. The edge cases with affiliates are where a lawyer should look.
- **Running it as a service:** a company can run a modified snapall on its servers for customers and never share the source. The AGPL closes that gap. It barely matters for a CLI tool.
- **Shipping it to others:** if they sell a binary, bundle it in a product, or hand it to a client, they must give *those recipients* the matching source under the GPL. They can't add restrictions, and those recipients may pass it on. They do **not** have to publish it publicly or send it to you. Only the people who received copies can ask for it.

So a company can keep a fork private, or share it selectively. The only unavoidable consequence is that anyone they ship it to can see and redistribute it. When they do convey it, they must also keep the notices and mark their changes, can't relicense it as proprietary, and must give the GPL's patent grant and installation information for locked-down consumer devices.

That's the same point as before: the GPL guarantees recipients' freedoms, not a flow of patches back to you. I'm not a lawyer.

That wait is **not related to snapall**. Your log shows the package built and passed all its tests, then `makepkg` stopped at the very last step, `pacman -U`.

## What the message means

`makepkg -i` prints "Pacman is currently in use, please wait..." whenever the lock file `/var/lib/pacman/db.lck` exists, and it keeps waiting. It only checks that the file exists, not whether a pacman process is actually running. The usual causes are:

- A **stale lock** left by a pacman that was interrupted (Ctrl+C at the wrong moment, a closed terminal, a crash, a power loss).
- A **background process** holding it, such as a GUI updater, PackageKit, or an update timer.

## How to find out which

Press Ctrl+C to stop the waiting `makepkg`; the package is already built. Then run:

```sh
ls -l /var/lib/pacman/db.lck               # does the lock exist?
pgrep -a 'pacman|pamac|packagekit|paru|yay'   # is something running?
sudo lsof /var/lib/pacman/db.lck           # who holds it, if anyone
```

- **A process shows up:** let it finish, or stop it. Don't delete the lock under a running pacman, because that can corrupt the package database.
- **Nothing shows up:** the lock is stale, and removing it is safe:

```sh
sudo rm /var/lib/pacman/db.lck
```

```sh
sudo pacman -U snapall-0.4.2-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst
```

## Check that the interrupted run left nothing half-done

If that run was a system upgrade, it may have been cut off partway. Look at what pacman was doing at that time:

```sh
grep '2026-10-22T21:' /var/log/pacman.log | tail -n 25
```

- **The last lines say `transaction completed`:** nothing was interrupted, and the lock was just left behind afterwards.
- **A `starting full system upgrade` or `transaction started` with no `transaction completed` after it:** the upgrade was cut off. Run `sudo pacman -Syu` (the full upgrade, not `-Sy` alone) and let it finish.
- **The interruption fell during kernel or `mkinitcpio` hook lines:** also run `sudo mkinitcpio -P` afterwards, so the boot images match the installed kernels.

- **Older snapshots.** Snapshots taken before the tool is installed can never be booted.
- **Encryption.** LUKS works, but the kernel and initramfs sit outside the encrypted partition.
- **Safe to automate.** The one safe step, enabling the service, turned out to be unnecessary, as the false warning showed.
- **Testing.** I can't test a bootloader change without booting virtual machines for every combination, and a failure leaves a machine that won't start. If such a test ever exists for one narrow setup, the ADR says to revisit.

## Is `/home` being snapshotted?
No. snapall snapshots every snapper config that exists, and a config is one Btrfs subvolume. A snapshot stops at a subvolume boundary, so on CachyOS the `root` config contains none of `/home` (it's a separate subvolume, `@home`).

Your TUI shows only `root` because that's the only config you have. There's no "all" row. The `a` key (or the `a all` button) snapshots every config.

I reproduced your symptom on real Btrfs, and it exposed my bug. I decided which config covers a file by path prefix, so a file in `/home` was attributed to `root`. The history then said "did not exist" in every snapshot, which was false: the file could never have been there.

**The fix:**
- **Coverage is now asked of the filesystem.** Each Btrfs subvolume has its own device number.
- **A file on another subvolume gets a clear error** naming the config, plus the exact command to give it snapshots.
- **`doctor` now warns** when a separate Btrfs `/home` has no config.
- **The README now says** what a snapshot contains.

## The answer

Until now nothing linked the snapshots that `a` makes in each area, so there was nothing to restore them together by. The design:

- **Restore point:** every snapshot made by one action (`snapall` or `a`) now carries the same tag, named after the time it started, e.g. `20261025T181500Z`.
- **Restore everything:** `snapall points` lists them, and `sudo snapall restore-all POINT` puts every area back at once. It supports `--dry-run`, and asks first unless you pass `--yes`.
- **Undo:** each area takes a safety snapshot first, and those form a restore point of their own. The command prints the one line that undoes the whole thing.
- **Your older snapshots:** ones made before the tag existed are grouped when they share a description and were taken within two minutes. They're labelled "matched by name and time" so a guess never looks like a fact.
- **One limit you should know about:** the running system (`root`) can't be put back while it runs (ADR 12). `restore-all` restores every other area and says plainly that the system is left alone, with the boot-menu route.

I've answered the Limine and theme questions and built the foundation of the Health work. The window tabs, status bar and Activity view are designed but not built yet.

## Your questions
**Rolling back a bad KDE/GNOME/Qt/GTK theme:**
- **Where themes live:** the settings are in your home folder, so this is the Home area. Restoring Home needs no reboot and no Limine.
- **Log out and back in:** do it after restoring. Desktops and apps rewrite their settings from memory when they exit, and GNOME's settings database is kept running in memory. I couldn't test any desktop here, so treat this as general knowledge, not something I verified.
- **System-wide themes:** a theme installed with your package manager lives under `/usr`, which is the system area. That one does need the boot-menu route.

**Restore all and root:**
- **What it restores:** `restore-all` puts back every area except the running system, because a running system can't safely replace itself (ADR 12).
- **When Limine is needed:** only if the bad change involved root, for example a package update.

**Can Limine show grouped restore points?** No, not out of the box.
- **What it lists:** Limine's menu follows snapper's **root** snapshots only, and each entry is one snapshot of one area. In my search I found no sign of support for other areas.
- **Practical order:** pick the root snapshot of your point in the Limine menu and boot it, then run `limine-snapper-restore`. After that, run `sudo snapall restore-all POINT` again for the other areas.
- **Output change:** restore-all now names the number of the system's snapshot in that point and says what order to do things in.

## What's built
- **ADR 16** records the design:
  - **Tabs:** Snapshots, Restore points, Health, Activity.

  - **Status bar:** it appears on every tab, and each item is clickable.

- **Running it:** `snapall health` gives a verdict first, then what to do about each thing (most urgent first), then the numbers.

- **Verified:** 374 tests pass on real Btrfs, and I ran it on a real filesystem with quotas off, with quotas on, and with the disk at 85%.

**Measured, not assumed:**
- **Quotas:** the room each snapshot holds exists only when Btrfs quotas are on. Otherwise the report says "not measured" and why, never a guess.
- **Shared space:** space shared by two snapshots belongs to neither, because Btrfs frees deleted snapshots lazily. The real-Btrfs test waits for that explicitly.
- **Cleanup status:** "cleanup on" means its timer is enabled and running.

**1. Quotas.**
- **Where:** the window has a switch (Enter on the "Counting the room snapshots take" row), and the command line has `snapall quotas [on|off]`. Both explain first and ask before changing anything.
- **What it gives:** it shows what each snapshot alone holds, and lets cleanup act on room as well as on counts.
- **What it costs:** the disk keeps a tally, which the kernel's own notes call a known slowdown when snapshots are deleted.
- **My recommendation:** leave it off if you have few snapshots and don't need their size, and the text says so. It is never switched on silently.
- **Only the full kind is offered.** The newer "simple" kind is cheap but charges room to whoever wrote it first, so it cannot say what a snapshot holds.
- **Verified on real Btrfs:** it showed 2.9 MiB held for a deleted 3 MB file.

**2. Jobs.** The Health tab lists each job from one catalogue, with its real name, state, and the schedule and description from its own unit file. Enter opens its controls: enable, disable, start, stop, restart and run-now, each beside the exact command it stands for, plus the status and log commands.

**3. Cleanup text.** It is built from the unit file's schedule and each area's real limits. The old text said "50" and "once a day". A test changes the inputs and checks the text changes with them, and that nothing is invented when nothing is known.

**7. Rollbacks.** Restoring an area puts back everything in it, including programs' settings, saved sessions, databases and logs, and an open program can overwrite the restored files. Every restore prompt now says so and says what to do. The structural fix is Btrfs's own: a snapshot stops at a subvolume boundary, so data that must never roll back (caches, VMs, logs) belongs in its own subvolume. The README says this.

**8. "Working".** The header now counts seconds. The line under the status bar names the change in progress. After five seconds it leads with "This can take a while; waiting is safe."

**9. Races.** One change at a time across the window and every changing command. A second one is refused and told who holds the lock and what for; reading is never blocked. I tested it against a real second process. It only guards snapall from snapall, not from snapper or other tools.

## What I decided differently from how you asked (10–12 and 6)
I would not build a resident daemon. It adds an always-running privileged surface and a second code path for a few seconds of work now and then. Instead, jobs would run as transient systemd units, with a small journal under `/var/lib/snapall/jobs/`. That gives jobs that survive closing the window, history across sessions, a Jobs view and a status-bar chip, with no process running while idle. Aborting would be cooperative, stopping between areas and never mid-restore. The reasoning is in ADR 17. If you still want the resident daemon, it can sit on the same journal. This is the next step, and it also fixes the fact that Activity still shows only the current session.

## What's new
- **Stopping protection.** Run `snapall unprotect AREA`, or press **`U` on an area's row** in the Health tab. The area's own files are untouched, and protecting it again later starts fresh with no snapshots.
- **It checks what it deletes before it does anything.** I tested on real snapper: removing an area's config deletes its `.snapshots` folder and every snapshot, and leaves the area's files alone. So the warning can be exact.
- **A plan comes first.** The window and the command line show the same wording, built from one plan:
  - how many snapshots will be deleted;
  - how much room that frees, when room is measured;
  - how many restore points stop including the area;
  - which groups name it.
  
  The plan is recomputed at the moment of doing, not trusted from when the prompt opened.
- **You must type the area's name.** A `y` or Enter is not enough. `--yes` is for scripts, and `--dry-run` only shows the plan.
- **The system area is refused.** The check runs when planning and again when acting, so nothing can reach the deletion without passing it. A forged plan for the system area is refused too. Its snapshots are what the boot menu offers and how you get back from a bad update.
- `U` is a key of its own, never the Enter that other rows use for milder things.

- **Three weights, one table**, read by the command line, the window and the tests:

  - **Restore:** goes back to the snapshot it took just before.
  - **Limits and groups:** go back to the numbers and areas they had.
  - **Protecting an area:** goes back to not protected.
  - **Taking a snapshot:** goes back by deleting it, so it needs `destroy`.
  - **Not undoable:** a deleted snapshot, or an area that stopped being protected, cannot be undone, and the record says so and what protects you next time (a snapshot or `snapall create --group`).
- **`snapall undo CHANGE`** shows the state it returns to, re-checks that it still exists (cleanup may have removed it), asks at the weight of what it does, and runs the recorded commands. `snapall activity` shows the way back under each change, in text and JSON.

## What I think
The condition that decides whether it works is that the top layer must be the code that *runs*, or what the running code is derived from. A "prose" module that only mirrors the real logic drifts exactly like a comment, only with more ceremony. If the layer could be deleted and the program stay unchanged, it was prose.

- The facts about what an act is, weighs, is called and which flags answer it were kept in four places, held together by tests. A test shows two copies agree; it doesn't remove the second copy.

So "tied by tests" isn't enough. The better tool is to declare a fact once and derive the rest, and to use tests only where derivation is impossible.

## What I built
- **`Act` is the app's vocabulary:** every act is listed once, with its weight and its title.
- **Each command declares what it does** (`.does(Act::DeleteSnapshots)`). Whether it takes `--yes` or `--destroy` is now *derived* from the weight of those acts, not declared again. I compared the contract with the old one for all 36 inputs: identical.
- **The window is derived from it too:** each question's title comes from `Act::title`, typed at no call site, and a button now says what it is for. A button looks dangerous because what it is for loses something for good, not because a list names `Delete`.
- **A ratchet on handler length.** No handler may exceed 60 lines. The six that do are listed at their present length; none may grow, no new one may join, and each must leave the list once it is short enough. I proved it bites by planting a 72-line function.
- **ADR 19 records the rule.** It covers the stepdown layers (purpose, acts, changes, steps), derive rather than verify, make the wrong state unrepresentable (exhaustive matches and typestate), and a function reads as a sentence. It also says what is *not* claimed: not everything reads as prose, and a layer of names that only renames the layer below is indirection, not clarity.

## Where I'd sharpen your idea
- **Each layer is a small language.** It has nouns (states, as types), verbs (actions, as functions) and a story that composes the layer below. The recursion stops where the language isn't ours, and each foreign thing is wrapped once, at the bottom, in our words. This is the "stratified design" of Abelson and Sussman's SICP, so it has a solid pedigree.
- **A front file is a map, not "everything in one place".** It lists what exists, with logic left to the modules it names. If it grows past a screen, a level is missing.
- **For inputs and outputs to be literally in one place, they must be values.** Handlers *return* what to show and one presenter prints. Then each surface is exactly "input enum → story → output enum". Today handlers print.
- **The prose must be generated from the code**, or it drifts again.

## The concept in one sentence
**Every layer of a program is a small language, written in the words of the layer above it and built from the layer below it, so reading the code from the top teaches the whole app, and nothing is written a second time that could drift.**

This is in `docs/canon/small-languages.md` in the snapall repo, with ADR 19 and ADR 20 recording the decisions. I haven't copied it to your canon repo yet, because you're still refining it.

## The idea
- **Nouns, verbs, story.** A layer has nouns (the states it can be in, as types) and verbs (the actions it offers, as functions). It also has a story: how its verbs are made of the verbs of the layer below.
- **Stopping at the boundary.** The stack ends where the language isn't ours: the compiler, other crates, the operating system, the tools we call. There, each foreign thing is wrapped once, in our words, and nothing above the wrapper names it.
- **Where it comes from.** This is stratified design (Abelson and Sussman), information hiding, deep modules, ports and adapters, the stepdown rule and a ubiquitous language, held together as one discipline.

## The sixteen rules, grouped
**How a module presents itself**
- **R1:** a module states what it is for in one sentence.
- **R2:** a front file is a map, not contents (120 lines at most). If it grows, a level is missing.
- **R9:** a file is one thing (300 lines at most).
- **R12:** prose may name, only code may claim. A purpose is a noun phrase; guarantees ("only", "never") go in tests.

**What goes in names and layers**
- **R3:** names are the person's words ("area", "snapshot", "restore point"), never a pattern word (`Manager`) or a tool's word (`config`, `snapper`) above the adapters.
- **R4:** a story calls only the layer below. It reads as ask, do, record, say.
- **R7:** each foreign thing is wrapped once, at the bottom.
- **R16:** a reader learns by reading downwards. Each word is defined before it is used, and the domain is taught by its types. The test is a cold read: someone given only the outline and front files should be able to say what the program does.

**What logic lives where**
- **R11:** each layer owns a kind of logic. The top keeps only *which, when and where*: branching, ordering, arrangement, streaming. The *how* lives lower. A top-layer line reads as common sense and is also the real running code.
- **R14:** a story has a grammar. Each line is `noun = verb(noun, noun)`, with no format strings, `Option` plumbing, bare `bool`s or `None`s. Budgets: at most 4 turns and 2 closures. What Rust syntax is left in a story marks a *missing noun* (a `Stop`, an `Approved`, a `Said`). That is how the next layer is found.
- **R15:** arrangement is data at the top ("tabs above page above status above buttons"). Cell numbers live below.

**How it cannot drift**
- **R5:** derive, don't restate. Declare a fact once and compute the rest. A test that compares two hand-written copies is a smell: remove a copy.
- **R6:** a surface is `input → story → output`, with both ends enumerations. Handlers return what to show and one presenter prints.
- **R8:** make the wrong state unrepresentable. Match exhaustively with no catch-all, and carry an order in a type (an `Approved` value, so a change can't be made unasked).
- **R10:** prose is generated, from the module sentences and the contract.
- **R13:** the *why* has three carriers, and none is a comment: names and types, executable facts (tests named as sentences that run against the real tool), and the generated outline. Comments are only machine-readable annotations. A reason no carrier holds is a missing name or test.

## Procedure and honesty
The canon includes how to add a feature, where code goes, how to pay down a ratchet, templates, a worked example (`snapall delete`, 55 → 19 lines), anti-patterns (a prose layer that doesn't run, a growing front file, pass-through layers, names by pattern, over-splitting) and what's not settled. The size bounds are judgement; returning outputs as values pays off only where there are two surfaces or output worth testing.

- **Enforced by machine:**

Good question, and worth thinking through rather than just answering.

**What a release per merge actually buys.** Each one costs me about 8 minutes of waiting (four workflows, the package repositories, the install checks) and a few dozen runner-minutes. In return: a fresh version number for users, and early proof that publishing still works. But the second benefit is mostly already covered: CI builds the static packages and runs them on 11 distributions on *every* pull request. And for users, ten patch versions an hour is noise, not value, for a tool they'll update monthly. The only thing a per-merge release proves that CI can't is the **publishing step itself**, and that only changes when packaging or the release workflows change.

**The decision: batch.** `release-plz` already keeps a single release pull request open and updates it as changes land, so batching needs no new tool. It means my `ship.py` should stop merging that pull request every time. It should merge it when:
1. enough changes have piled up (default **10**, as you suggested), or
2. the changes touch **packaging or the release workflows**, so the publishing path gets verified right away, or
3. it's asked to explicitly.

## Why per-merge releases weren't worth it
Each release cost about eight minutes of waiting, four workflows and a few dozen runner-minutes. It gave users a new patch version every few minutes, for a tool they'd update monthly.

The only thing a per-merge release proved beyond what CI already proves was the **publishing step**. CI already builds the packages and runs them on 11 distributions on every pull request, and publishing only changes when packaging or the release workflows change. Extra releases also meant more chances for a flaky release job. One failed this week on a GitHub server error.

## What it does now (merged)
`release-plz` already keeps one release pull request open and updates it with each merge, so the only change was that my ship script stops merging that pull request every time. It now releases when:
- **10 changes** that make a changelog entry are waiting (chores and docs don't count), or
- the oldest waiting change is **7 days** old, or
- the change touches **packaging or the release workflows**, or
- I ask with `--release`.

Otherwise it says "release deferred: 2 of 10 changes are waiting" and moves on. When it does release, it first waits for the newest change to land in that pull request, so a batched release can't leave the latest change out.

I tested ten decisions, including one just under the limit and one just over, and confirmed the test fails when the threshold is off by one. It runs in the local gate and in CI. The cost is a bigger release when it comes, and a defect found by a release is found later. Both are small, since every change passes full CI first. The saving is real: a change now takes **two calls instead of six**.

"""The catalogue of guards, as functions: each reads source files and returns ``{name: number}``, which is exactly what ``ratchet.check`` takes.

    files_too_long(files)                      lines per file                                  (a file is short enough to read whole)
    entry_files_too_long(files)                lines per index file                            (an entry file only says what is in the folder)
    shared_purposes(modules)                   how many modules share a purpose sentence      (two modules cannot be for the same thing)
    jargon_purposes(modules)                   modules whose purpose uses a pattern word       (say what it is for, not what pattern it is)
    uses_outside(files, allowed, forbidden)    matches of a forbidden pattern outside the files allowed to have it   (purity by role)
    hand_spelled_plurals(files)                plurals spelled by hand                         (a helper says it, once)
    retired_word_uses(files, word, allowed)    identifiers that still contain a retired word  (checked on tokens, not text)

``files`` is ``{path: text}`` (``source_files`` reads it from folders; test files and inline test modules are left out), ``modules`` is the
outline's ``[(name, purpose)]``. A function that returns an empty dict has nothing to report; give the result to ``ratchet.check`` with a limit
(300 lines, 1 shared purpose, 0 for the rest) and the debts that cannot be paid yet become data that may only shrink. Ported from the tests in snapall's
``architecture.rs``; the lexer is a small one for C-like and Python sources, which is enough to tell a word in code from a word in a string.
"""
import os
import re

from outline import EXTENSIONS, SKIP_FILES

ENTRY_FILES = {"mod.rs", "lib.rs", "main.rs", "__init__.py", "index.ts", "index.js", "index.tsx"}
TESTS = ("/tests/", "/test/", "/__tests__/", "test_", "_test.", ".test.", ".spec.", "tests.rs")
STOP_AT = "#[cfg(test)]"
JARGON = re.compile(r"(adapter|imperative|\bshell\b|hexagon|composition root|functional core|driving|\bport\b)", re.I)


def source_files(roots, extensions=EXTENSIONS, tests=TESTS, stop_at=STOP_AT):
    """``{path: production text}`` for every source file under ``roots``."""
    found = {}
    for root in roots:
        for directory, _, names in os.walk(root):
            inside = os.path.relpath(directory, root).split(os.sep)
            if any((p.startswith(".") and p != ".") or p in ("node_modules", "target", "__pycache__") for p in inside):
                continue
            for name in names:
                path = os.path.join(directory, name)
                if name.rsplit(".", 1)[-1] not in extensions or any(t in "/" + path for t in tests):
                    continue
                try:
                    text = open(path, encoding="utf-8").read()
                except (UnicodeDecodeError, OSError):
                    continue
                if stop_at and stop_at.replace("#[", "#![") in text:
                    continue
                found[path] = text.split("\n" + stop_at)[0] if stop_at else text
    return found


def files_too_long(files):
    return {path: len(text.split("\n")) for path, text in files.items()}


def entry_files_too_long(files):
    return {path: len(text.split("\n")) for path, text in files.items() if os.path.basename(path) in ENTRY_FILES}


def shared_purposes(modules):
    count = {}
    for name, purpose in modules:
        if purpose and os.path.basename(name) not in SKIP_FILES:
            count[purpose] = count.get(purpose, 0) + 1
    return count


def jargon_purposes(modules):
    return {name: 1 for name, purpose in modules if purpose and JARGON.search(purpose)}


def uses_outside(files, allowed, forbidden):
    """``allowed`` and ``forbidden`` are regular expressions: the files whose path matches ``allowed`` may use what ``forbidden`` matches; elsewhere it is counted."""
    allowed, forbidden = re.compile(allowed), re.compile(forbidden)
    return {path: n for path, text in files.items() if not allowed.search(path) and (n := len(forbidden.findall(text)))}


PLURAL_IDIOMS = [
    re.compile(r"[=!]==?\s*1\s*\{\s*\"[^\"]*\"\s*\}\s*else\s*\{\s*\"[^\"]*\""),            # Rust: if n == 1 { "" } else { "s" }
    re.compile(r"[=!]==?\s*1\s*\?\s*[\"'][^\"']*[\"']\s*:\s*[\"']"),                        # JS, TS, Java, C: n === 1 ? "" : "s"
    re.compile(r"[\"'][^\"']*[\"']\s+if\s+\w+\s*[=!]=\s*1\s+else\s+[\"']"),                 # Python: "" if n == 1 else "s"
]


def hand_spelled_plurals(files):
    """The idiom in any words, and ``snapshot(s)`` inside a string, which leaves the plural to the reader."""
    found = {}
    for path, text in files.items():
        flat = " ".join(text.split())
        n = sum(len(idiom.findall(flat)) for idiom in PLURAL_IDIOMS)
        for hack in ("(s)", "(es)"):
            at = flat.find(hack)
            while at != -1:
                quotes = flat[:at].count('"') - flat[:at].count('\\"')
                if quotes % 2 == 1 and flat[:at][-1:].isalpha():  # inside a string, after a letter: ``Ok(s)`` in code is not one
                    n += 1
                at = flat.find(hack, at + 1)
        if n:
            found[path] = n
    return found


def identifiers(text, line_comment=("//", "#")):
    """The identifiers of ``text`` that are code: not inside a string, a character or a comment."""
    i, n = 0, len(text)
    while i < n:
        c = text[i]
        if text.startswith(line_comment, i):
            i = text.find("\n", i)
            i = n if i == -1 else i
        elif text.startswith("/*", i):
            i = text.find("*/", i + 2)
            i = n if i == -1 else i + 2
        elif c in "\"'":
            quote = c * 3 if text.startswith(c * 3, i) else c
            i += len(quote)
            while i < n and not text.startswith(quote, i):
                i += 2 if text[i] == "\\" else 1
            i += len(quote)
        elif c.isalpha() or c == "_":
            j = i
            while j < n and (text[j].isalnum() or text[j] == "_"):
                j += 1
            yield text[i:j]
            i = j
        else:
            i += 1


def _parts(identifier):
    return [p.lower() for p in re.findall(r"[A-Z]?[a-z0-9]+|[A-Z]+(?![a-z])", identifier.replace("_", " "))]


def retired_word_uses(files, word, allowed=None):
    """Identifiers that have ``word`` as one of their parts (``config``, ``area_config``, ``ConfigName``), outside the files matching ``allowed``."""
    allowed = re.compile(allowed) if allowed else None
    found = {}
    for path, text in files.items():
        if allowed and allowed.search(path):
            continue
        n = sum(1 for name in identifiers(text) if word.lower() in _parts(name) or word.lower() + "s" in _parts(name))
        if n:
            found[path] = n
    return found

sys.path.insert(0, HERE)

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    os.chdir(ROOT)
    files = rules.source_files(LAYERS.values())
    modules = outline.build(LAYERS)
    ratchet = os.path.join(ROOT, RATCHETS)
    check(f"Files longer than {MAX_FILE_LINES} lines (a file is short enough to read whole; split it by purpose, or record the debt):",
          "files_too_long", rules.files_too_long(files), MAX_FILE_LINES, path=ratchet)
    check(f"Entry files longer than {MAX_ENTRY_FILE_LINES} lines (an entry file only says what is in the folder):",
          "entry_files_too_long", rules.entry_files_too_long(files), MAX_ENTRY_FILE_LINES, path=ratchet)
    check("Modules that share a purpose sentence (two modules cannot be for the same thing; say what each is for):",
          "shared_purposes", rules.shared_purposes(modules), 1, path=ratchet)
    check("Modules whose first sentence uses a pattern word (say what it is for, not which pattern it is):",
          "jargon_purposes", rules.jargon_purposes(modules), 0, path=ratchet)
    check("Plurals spelled by hand (`if n == 1` in any words, or `thing(s)`): say it with one helper:",

    for word, allowed in RETIRED_WORDS.items():

              f"retired_{word}", rules.retired_word_uses(files, word, allowed), 0, path=ratchet)
    for i, (allowed, forbidden, what) in enumerate(ONLY_IN):
        check(f"Files that use {what} but are not allowed to:", f"only_in_{i}", rules.uses_outside(files, allowed, forbidden), 0, path=ratchet)
    return f"architecture: {len(files)} files, {len(modules)} modules: every guard holds"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        print(run())
    except RatchetError as error:
        print(error)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 grenudi
#
# SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-3.0-or-later

"""Look at the screens of a terminal program as a person would: run it in a pseudo-terminal, press keys, and print what is on the screen after each.

    screens.py [--size COLSxROWS] [--wait SECONDS] [--keys KEY,KEY,...] -- COMMAND [ARGS...]

Reading a program's code finds what is wrong with the code; only using the program finds what is wrong with what it says. For a command line that is
running it and reading the output. For a terminal UI it needs a terminal: this one runs the program in a pseudo-terminal of the given size (default
100x30), feeds the output to a terminal emulator (pyte), presses each key in turn, waits for the screen to settle, and prints it. A key is a single
character, or one of: enter, esc, tab, space, backspace, up, down, left, right, ctrl-c, ctrl-d.

    screens.py --keys 2,3,?,q -- ./target/debug/myapp tui        the first screen, then the screen after each key

Needs ``pip install pyte``. Output uses box-drawing characters: do not cut it with a byte-oriented tool (``cut``), or the stream is no longer UTF-8.
"""
import fcntl
import os
import pty
import select
import signal
import struct
import sys
import termios
import time

KEYS = {"enter": b"\r", "esc": b"\x1b", "tab": b"\t", "space": b" ", "backspace": b"\x7f", "ctrl-c": b"\x03", "ctrl-d": b"\x04",
        "up": b"\x1b[A", "down": b"\x1b[B", "right": b"\x1b[C", "left": b"\x1b[D"}


def key_bytes(name):
    if name in KEYS:
        return KEYS[name]
    if len(name) == 1:
        return name.encode()
    raise SystemExit(f"screens.py: unknown key {name!r}; a character or one of: {', '.join(KEYS)}")


class Terminal:
    """A program running in a pseudo-terminal, and the screen it has drawn."""

    def __init__(self, command, cols=100, rows=30, env=None):
        import pyte
        self.screen = pyte.Screen(cols, rows)
        self.stream = pyte.ByteStream(self.screen)
        self.pid, self.fd = pty.fork()
        if self.pid == 0:
            os.environ.update(env or {})
            os.environ.setdefault("TERM", "xterm-256color")
            os.execvp(command[0], command)
        fcntl.ioctl(self.fd, termios.TIOCSWINSZ, struct.pack("HHHH", rows, cols, 0, 0))

    def settle(self, wait=0.6, patience=4.0):
        """Read until the program has been quiet for ``wait`` seconds (or ``patience`` in all)."""
        end, quiet_since = time.time() + patience, time.time()
        while time.time() < end and time.time() - quiet_since < wait:
            ready, _, _ = select.select([self.fd], [], [], 0.05)
            if ready:
                try:
                    data = os.read(self.fd, 65536)
                except OSError:
                    return
                if not data:
                    return
                self.stream.feed(data)
                quiet_since = time.time()

    def press(self, key, wait=0.6):
        os.write(self.fd, key_bytes(key))
        self.settle(wait)

    def text(self):
        lines = [line.rstrip() for line in self.screen.display]
        while lines and not lines[-1]:
            lines.pop()
        return "\n".join(lines)

    def close(self):
        for sig in (signal.SIGTERM, signal.SIGKILL):
            try:
                os.kill(self.pid, sig)
                time.sleep(0.05)
                os.waitpid(self.pid, os.WNOHANG)
            except (ProcessLookupError, ChildProcessError):
                break


def main(argv):
    if "--" not in argv:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    split = argv.index("--")
    options, command = argv[:split], argv[split + 1:]

**What the documentation says.** Anthropic's API docs describe *compaction*. When a conversation approaches the context limit, the older part is automatically summarized, which extends the effective context length for long-running conversations. They also say compaction exists because as a conversation grows, response quality degrades, so older content is replaced with a concise summary. The limit itself is still there; it is managed rather than removed.

The best fit is **a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner on a dedicated machine, with the phone plugged into it**. The runner only makes outbound connections to GitHub. I would push a branch, GitHub builds the kernel, the machine flashes and tests the real phone, and I read the results through the API. That is the same loop I used with `ship.py`, with a phone at the end of it.

## What fits in GitHub
- **Kernel fork, pmaports fork and the test harness:** all fit. The upstream group already keeps public repos for the kernel fork, pmaports, nightly builds, and firmware repos including `firmware-xiaomi-surya`, so I'd build on those.
- **Builds:** GitHub's cloud runners cross-compile the kernel. Images go to Releases.
- **The phone and the tests:** these stay on your machine, which is why it needs the runner.

## What exists already
- **Speaker:** the SM7150 kernel got speaker support for xiaomi-surya in 6.13.2, so we have a working baseline to test against.
- **The gap:** the devices are generally very usable except for microphone/earpiece audio and cameras.
- **Where the kernel is:** the packaged kernel is at 7.1_rc3.

## How the test loop works
1. **Boot without installing.** The runner boots each test kernel with `fastboot boot`, so nothing is flashed and the stable system is never touched.
2. **Collect results.** It reaches the phone over USB networking, pulls `dmesg` and the audio card list, and runs tests.
3. **Check audio automatically.**
   - A cheap 3.5mm loopback plug lets the phone play a tone and record it back.
   - The runner checks the tone's frequency and level.
   - This proves the audio path works. It can't judge quality; you'd listen to that occasionally.
4. **Track progress as data.** A table of features (speaker, headphone, mic, earpiece, and so on) may only improve, as in the playbook.

## Why not SSH
My sandbox is temporary, and anything inbound to your machine needs port forwarding. The runner avoids that. A runner job can also take a command as input and return its output, which gives you remote execution without opening anything. For live debugging, Tailscale would work, but it needs a key pasted into this chat and is fragile.

- A dedicated Linux machine, a USB cable to the phone, a TRRS loopback plug, and the bootloader unlocked with pmOS installed.

- A **private repository** for the hardware tests. A public repo with a self-hosted runner would let anyone's fork run code on your machine.

## Real risks
- **Hung kernel:** a hard hang needs a power-button hold. Start with a human rescue, or add a $5 relay across the power button later.
- **Battery:** the phone sits plugged in and unattended, so I'd limit charge and watch temperature.
- **Token:** the classic GitHub token I've been using appears in this chat's history. Please rotate it afterwards and use a narrow, expiring one for this project.

def load(path=DEFAULT_PATH):
    try:
        with open(path, "rb") as f:
            raw = tomllib.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        raise ConfigError(f"no configuration at {path}")
    except tomllib.TOMLDecodeError as error:
        raise ConfigError(f"{path} is not valid TOML: {error}")
    return from_dict(raw, path)


def from_dict(raw, where="the configuration"):
    flat = {}
    for section, values in raw.items():
        if isinstance(values, dict) and section != "extra_env":
            flat.update({f"{section}_{k}" if section in ("jobs", "results") and k in ("remote", "branch", "dir") else k: v for k, v in values.items()})
        else:
            flat[section] = values
    known = {f.name: f for f in fields(Config)}
    for name in flat:
        if name not in known:
            raise ConfigError(f"{where}: unknown setting {name!r}; known: {', '.join(sorted(known))}")
    for required in ("jobs_remote", "results_remote"):
        if not flat.get(required):
            raise ConfigError(f"{where}: {required.replace('_', ' ')} is required (put `remote = ...` under [{required.split('_')[0]}])")
    for name, value in flat.items():
        want = type(known[name].default) if known[name].default is not None and not isinstance(known[name].default, type(None)) and name != "extra_env" else None
        if name == "extra_env":
            if not isinstance(value, dict):
                raise ConfigError(f"{where}: extra_env must be a table")
        elif want in (int, float) and (isinstance(value, bool) or not isinstance(value, (int, float))):
            raise ConfigError(f"{where}: {name} must be a number, not {value!r}")
        elif want is str and not isinstance(value, str):
            raise ConfigError(f"{where}: {name} must be text, not {value!r}")
    config = Config(**flat)
    if config.jobs_remote == config.results_remote:
        raise ConfigError(f"{where}: the jobs and results repositories must differ: the agent never writes where it reads")
    for name in ("poll_seconds", "push_seconds", "idle_heartbeat_seconds", "grace_seconds"):
        if getattr(config, name) <= 0:
            raise ConfigError(f"{where}: {name} must be above zero")
    if config.default_timeout > config.max_timeout:
        raise ConfigError(f"{where}: default_timeout is above max_timeout")
    return config
