**Stereo works on your phone.** You heard tone A from the top speaker and tone B from the bottom one, the first time the right channel has ever played.

**What was wrong.** The two speaker amplifiers expected each channel in a 32-bit "slot", but the phone's audio processor sends 16-bit slots. So each amp read the whole stereo frame as its left channel, and the right channel fell past the end of the frame into silence. It compiles for the phone's architecture and is pushed to your kernel fork as its own branch, `fix/tas2562-i2s-slot-length`, with a full explanation in the commit. It's a good upstream candidate, and you'll be its author when we send it.

Localization is worth getting right, because it touches every page. The key insight is that the site holds **two different kinds of text**, and they deserve different mechanisms.

**1. The interface:** headings, navigation, legends, "commits in the last 90 days". It belongs to the **face**, so it should use **proper message catalogs**. The best of the best here is **Project Fluent** (Mozilla's localization system). It's the right choice over simple string tables because of **grammar**. Russian has three plural forms: *1 коммит, 2 коммита, 5 коммитов*. A plain "N commits" → "N коммитов" table gets that wrong two times out of three. Fluent handles it correctly for every language, and it's a mature Rust crate.

**2. The data:** titles, goals, notes, milestones, concepts. It belongs to the **projects**. Translations should **never touch the source tables** (that would muddle "data made by work"). Instead each project gets a standard ocoeco table, **`translations`**: which table, row and column, in which language, the text, and **who translated it**, human or machine, so an agent's translation is never passed off as a person's. Anything untranslated **falls back to the source language**: a partly translated page is still a whole page. Same principle as "unknown is not failure".

**The site structure:** exactly as you said, the same static files multiplied per language, under **`/en/` and `/ru/`**, with identical paths. Two refinements make it best of the best:
- **The old addresses keep working.** Every page at the root becomes a tiny redirect to its `/en/` twin, so no existing link breaks.
- **Every page declares its language and its translations** (`lang`, `hreflang`). Browsers, screen readers and search engines then know which is which.

**The switcher:** your thin line is right. It goes at the **right end of the header**, on every page, where people look for it. Each language appears in its **own name**, **English · Русский**, with no flags (flags mean countries, not languages) and no codes a reader might not recognize. The current language shows in bold, and the other links to **the same page** in that language.

You asked me to reflect on this and not just accept it, so here's what I actually think, including where I disagree.

**1. Adding `-oco` to everything: I'd push back, and your own manifesto is the reason.** Rhizome's first "mistake" is *identifying things by name*. Belonging to the ecosystem is already declared the right way: by the **mark**, which a machine reads and which survives any rename, and by the `oco-project` **topic**, which a person sees as a badge on every repo's GitHub page. Encoding membership in names as well would repeat the mistake we're trying to leave behind. It also has real costs: package names, install commands and links all change. Where a suffix *does* earn its place is on **organizations**: there are few of them, they're the roofs people land on, and plain names are often taken (`rhizome-oco`, `linux-phone-oco`). So my recommendation is orgs yes, where it helps; repos, tools and commands no. I also accepted "lab-agent → lab-agent-oco" too quickly last turn, and I'd now keep the command as `lab-agent`. If you still want `creation-guidelines-oco` as an org name, that one is cheap and I'll do it. But I wouldn't ripple it downward.

**2. "How it works" belongs to every project: you're right, and it's better than what I proposed.** My "one roof" made *how we work* a special thing floating beside the projects. Yours makes it a **standard part of every project**, like its backlog and milestones. That completes a chain I hadn't seen whole:

> **Idea** (why this exists) → **Path** (what it must reach) → **Workings** (how each step is delivered and proven, and by which tools) → **Work** (what actually happened)

The workings aren't a random toolbox. Each one **serves a milestone** and **produces evidence**: "this check proves that milestone; this gatherer feeds that number; we care because…". Shared tools like `land` or `devlab` are just projects that other projects *point at* in their workings, the same chaining the paths already use. And then the observatory is, as you say, **just another project following ocoeco**. That's the test of a good system.

**3. The Idea tab: you're right, and the fault is mine.** What I wrote there are terse spec-style cards, alphabetically ordered, in my voice. They tell an insider what the parts are called; they tell a commoner nothing about *what this is and why it matters to them*. Your gists do the opposite: they start from the reader's own experience, use analogies, and are honest about limits. The idea should be the project's own, kept in its own repo, as **an ordered piece of writing**, not a pile of cards. The lens only gathers and shows it.

On the shells and packaging, here's my honest picture of the best version, including where I'd push back.

**What I fully agree with:**
- **Owning our versions of the shells** turns "fixes we keep in our heads" into something that ships.
- **One packaging conveyor that every project uses,** instead of copy-pasted CI, is exactly the right instinct. It's the same shape as ocoeco's gatherer: projects *call* a shared workflow and pin its version, and nobody copies it.

**Where I'd shape it differently:**
1. **A fork should be "upstream plus a small, named stack of patches," never a divergent copy.** Every patch is written to go home, and carries its upstream status. The fork is rebased onto upstream automatically, and our CI tells us the day a patch stops applying. That is what a rhizcut *means*, and it's the only way three shells stay affordable. A drifting fork of three large projects would eat the whole effort.
2. **One shell first, end to end; then the others as copies of a proven pattern.** The phone runs **Sxmo**, so that's the first instance: patch → build → our package repository → installed on the phone → health checks pass. The other two follow the same template.
3. **The conveyor must target what the machines actually run.** The phone runs postmarketOS, which uses Alpine's `apk` packages. The lab machine runs Arch and `pacman` (that's how snapall and lab-agent ship today). So `linux-package-distribution-oco` should support both from one declaration, with a signed repository for each, and grow other formats later.
4. **Rhizoid's own tool isn't built yet.** So these rhizcuts will be honest early ones: a fork pinned to an exact upstream point, carrying Rhizoid's cutting note, kept in sync by CI. That makes them Rhizoid's first real users too, which is good for Rhizoid.
5. **The lenses: one curated "Mobile shells" lens rather than three new tabs.** Each shell org still gets its own lens, discovered and listed. The curated tab shows them side by side: which bugs each carries, which patches went home, which works on the phone. Three tabs for forks that don't build yet would be painting the car again. Yes, we're on the same page, and you've corrected two things I got wrong. Here's the clearer picture.

**1. "Deliberate" was the wrong idea. Looking, listening and deciding are automatable too.**
- **Looking** at a screenshot becomes visual checks: perceptual image comparison against an approved picture (Rust has good tools for this, such as `dssim` and `image-compare`), plus layout checks run in the headless browser.
- **Listening** is spectrum analysis on established libraries (`rustfft` / `spectrum-analyzer`), not my hand-rolled detection. Our `devlab hear` uses `tone`, a small detector we wrote ourselves, and it should stand on those libraries instead.
- **Deciding** often becomes a rule written once. What truly needs a person should be rare, and it should be counted, not exempted.

This matters most for exactly your reason: **test suites must run start to finish without a person judging in the middle.** Toyota's word for this is *jidoka*: the machine judges, and stops itself on anything abnormal. So *deliberate* is gone. Everything is either manual or automated, and **effort decides what gets automated first.**

That settles it, so here's my thinking on both questions.

**1. Making our tools usable by agents.** The protocol is **MCP, the Model Context Protocol**: an open standard through which a program offers its abilities to any agent. Blender, Photoshop, GIMP and Aseprite are reached this way. For **interactive terminal programs** like our new picker, people have built MCP servers that run the program in a pseudo-terminal, send keys, **read the screen through a real terminal model**, and wait until expected text appears. That's the descendant of the classic `expect` from 1990. The two I found are Python, so not for us. The Rust pieces exist, though: a pseudo-terminal crate, a terminal-emulator crate, and MCP's official Rust SDK.

What I think is best, in three layers:
1. **Two doors for every tool.** The interactive door is for people; a structured door (plain arguments, machine-readable output) is for agents and scripts. `ocoeco manual "action"` beside the picker is already this. It's argenv's own idea, *one setting, two doors*, applied to whole tools. An agent should rarely need to drive a screen at all.
2. **A terminal driver for checking the interactive doors themselves:** start the program, press keys, wait for text, take the screen as text. That's exactly what my failed picker check needed.
3. **The conveyor:** projects declare **scenes** (scripted interactions with expected screens), the conveyor runs them in CI, and the screens become evidence, called rather than copied, like the packaging conveyor. **3. Parked.** Every item in progress, in five projects, is back to *open* with its resume point. The observatory holds the order to resume in, so nothing is lost.

**4. Redesigned,** now in lab-agent's data and `DESIGN.md`. **The root of the whole chain is one thing: a job had no record of its own life.** "Pending" was guessed from a missing result. Nothing held a lease, nothing sent a heartbeat, nothing watched from outside, and jobs shared working copies. The world solved these long ago, and the design takes their best ideas:
- **Every job keeps a journal** (submitted, claimed, heartbeats, steps done, finished), and the journal is the only truth. **A finished job can never start again,** and an unclaimed one expires.
- **Your heartbeat idea is the centre: the driver's lease.** While a session drives the lab, its client sends beats automatically. **If the beats stop, the agent starts nothing new, parks running work at its next step, and waits** to be told to resume.
- **Work is a flow of steps, each journalled when done.** After any interruption, it **resumes at the next step and never replays.** A rollout over 21 repositories would pick up at the 13th.
- **Each job gets its own working copy,** and jobs run side by side only when they need different things.
- **Crash-only:** a reboot or reconnect is never a special case, because the agent just reads its journal.
- **A voice of its own:** a watcher outside the machine (a scheduled GitHub workflow) alerts you when the agent goes silent.
- **The token leaves URLs** and gets rotated.
- **Everything flows through ocoeco.**

**Why not adopt an engine like Temporal:** it would need a server to run and secure, while lab-agent's world is one machine, no open ports, and git as its record. So it takes their proven ideas into a small Rust core, and **chaos tests prove each point**: kill it mid-step, reboot, reconnect, cut the network, and silence the driver.

**Next: stage 1, "safety first".** It closes every path the incident took: run-once, the driver's lease, the outside watcher, and an alarm that doesn't need the agent. Each piece is proven by a chaos test before the next stage.

- **The port** is the interface the core defines in its own terms, such as "a journal of jobs" or "a channel to the author".
- **The adapter** is one way of fulfilling it: GitHub today, Redis or anything else tomorrow.
- **The core never knows which adapter it's talking to.**

The design I wrote doesn't say that clearly enough, and it treats git as the database. You're right that git is today's transport, not the store.

**You also caught something about tad I need to be honest about.** The Rust tad I built *dropped SQL*. I declared tables as data and treated SQL as "a possible view, later". If tad is to be lab-agent's store, it needs **real queries**, so that gap is now on the critical path.

Looking first at what the playbook and the canon actually say, so the design follows them rather than my memory of them:

Both are landed.

**lab-agent's design now follows the canon and the playbook:**
- **Its core speaks its own language** (work, steps, the journal, the driver's lease, the author, the voice) and **depends on nothing outside itself.** It'll be a crate with no input or output, so the compiler holds the line.
- **GitHub, git, ntfy and systemd are today's adapters,** and their words appear nowhere above them. Replacing git with Redis means writing a new adapter that passes the same checks the in-memory one passes, and **the core doesn't change.**
- **Areas are named for what lab-agent is for:** taking work, doing it, keeping the journal, holding leases, resuming, speaking, listening, watching. Never "ports" or "services".
- **The playbook's guards check all of this on every change,** and in-memory stand-ins run the chaos tests.

**The journal is data, not a heap of files:**
- **It's declared tad tables:** jobs, their events, steps, leases, your messages, waits. Where they live is itself an adapter: git today, a database later.
- **Every finished piece of work becomes a glimpse,** so what the hands did is intelligible across the commons.

**tad gets real SQL back,** and I've recorded honestly that dropping it was wrong.
- **Through an embedded SQLite:** queries read the declared tables, and changes are checked by tad before anything is kept, as the Python version did.
- **It's to be proven equal** on the four repositories' own queries before anything relies on it.

2. **tad's SQL,** with its equivalence proof, since the journal depends on it.
3. **The new core, stage by stage,** starting with *safety first*: run-once, the driver's lease with park-on-silence, the outside watcher, and an alarm that doesn't need the agent. Each piece is proven by a chaos test before the next.

Continuing with **the runner**: the part of oco-agent that actually does the work. Here's the design, in plain words.

**The core says what to do; the runner carries it out through "hands".** The hands are a port: start a job, look at how it's going, stop it, and clear what a dead run left behind. Today's adapter is *processes on this machine*. A container or a remote machine would be another adapter, and the core wouldn't change.

**Every start, end, timeout and parking is written into the journal as it happens,** so the journal is always the truth about what ran:
- **A job is claimed in the journal *before* it starts.** If the claim is refused, it doesn't start. That's run-once, enforced at the moment of action.
- **Each job declares how long it may run.** If it overstays, it's stopped and recorded as *timed out*.
- **A job that can't start is recorded as *failed* and not retried.**

**Crash-only, done properly: a job owns everything it starts.** Every process a job launches carries the job's name as a mark in its environment. So when a job ends, is stopped, or was left behind by a dead runner, *everything* carrying its mark is ended. Nothing lingers to collide with a later run.

I weighed process groups, which a job's children can leave, and "kill on parent death", which only covers the direct child. The mark covers grandchildren too.

**Two smaller decisions:**
- **A job's name must be safe as a file name.** That closes a path-traversal hole before it exists.
- **The journal's adapter now owns its declaration.** That way the shadow's existing journal upgrades cleanly when a field is added, such as how long a job may run.

Continuing with **speaking: what happened goes back to the repository**, so you or I can see from anywhere how work went.

**The design, in plain words:**
- **One repository, two branches.** `main` holds what was *asked*. A branch called `spoken` holds what *happened*: the journal, and each job's log. The asking history stays clean, a driver needs only one repository, and the watcher on `main` is undisturbed.
- **Written only when something changed:**
  - **The journal** at most every 10 seconds.
  - **A running job's log** at most once a minute.
  - **A finished job's log** at once.

  That respects both GitHub budgets, the request budget and the stricter one for commits.
- **Logs before the journal.** When a driver reads that a job ended, its log is already there.
- **Only jobs this run touched are spoken.** A restarted runner doesn't burst old logs out.
- **The driver gains `standing`, `log` and `wait` with `--via`.** **Waiting counts as being present,** so `wait` beats every minute and your lease stays alive while you watch your own job. Exit codes say how the job ended.

**Speaking works, and oco-agent can now be driven entirely from anywhere:**

```
$ oco-agent wait spoken-ok-… --via grenudi/lab-agent-jobs
line one
line two, the end
spoken-ok-… finished          (exit 0)

$ oco-agent wait spoken-bad-… --via …
this one fails
spoken-bad-… failed           (exit 1)
```

**The research behind the board, the best of what exists:**
- **Kanban** (Anderson, from Toyota): make the flow visible, limit work in progress, pull rather than push, make policies explicit, and watch how long items sit still.
- **Reinertsen's flow principles:** queues are the hidden cost, and work that ages is the warning.
- **GitHub Projects and Linear:** items stored *once*, with many views over them. **The board is a view, never a second list.**

- **The board is a query over every project's backlog.** No separate list.

That confirms the essence, and it's striking how well it fits:

- Obeya began because Uchiyamada understood that no single individual possessed the depth of knowledge required for the Prius.

The "command centre" language and score boards came later. That's the layer to leave out.

## What you mean, as I understand it

**The board isn't a list of tasks. It's the room.** For open commons, ocoeco is the next step of Obeya: one place where anyone sees the whole, covering purpose, knowledge, reasoning, work, results and problems. And it should be learned by *seeing and touching*, not by cramming.

**I was too narrow.** I kept treating the backlog as the centre because it was the first thing we built. It's one wall.

## Three things I see when I take the wide view

**1. ocoeco's entities already *are* the walls of the room.** Nothing new needs inventing:

| Wall of the room | What ocoeco already keeps |
|---|---|
| Purpose | the idea, milestones |
| Knowledge | research, sources, concepts, vocabulary |
| Reasoning | decisions, with what was rejected |
| Work | the backlog's flow |
| Results | glimpses, workings and their evidence |
| Looking back | reflections |
| Problems | "what needs attention" (computed today, not yet a wall of its own) |

**2. Your four words and the room are one design, not two.**
- **A wall is a lens.**
- **The room is what an observer shows of a constellation.**

So **"board" needs no entity of its own.** The flow I built is simply one lens among others. This is the simplification you're asking for: three things we had planned separately turn out to be the same thing, **a lens declared as data** (queries plus how they're shown). Those three are the renderer leaving tad, "presentation as data", and the observatory engine's 4,000 lines of hand-written views.

**3. Open commons need one wall Toyota never did.** In a company, people are *assigned*. In a commons, nobody is, so **the room must also invite**: it shows what's needed from whoever walks in. A piece of information, a test on a device they own, feedback. That's your picture of users adding their part, and it's the specifically *open commons* contribution to the idea.

## On star, constellation, lens, observer

**It's not too big, and it holds together.** The four words each name a distinct part, and the astronomy fits the observatory. I'd adopt them. Two points must be faced for it to work, and one collision:

- **A view across stars can't be made from renders.** "What is in progress across the whole constellation" needs the stars' *data*, not their rendered pages. The resolution keeps your rule intact: such a view is **a lens of the constellation**, run once over its stars' data and rendered there. **Observers still only gather renders.**
- **Gathering renders needs a small agreement on what a render *is***: which lens, which format, where it starts. Without it, an observer can't place what it gathers. That agreement is the protocol.
- **"Lens" already means something here**: today it names a *kind of project* (a subject area). That older meaning becomes **constellation**. One nice consequence: a star can belong to several constellations, where today a project has a single parent.

Yes, I see it more clearly now, and I think your last message contains the answer to both things you're unsure of. Here is the full picture as I see it.

## Three kinds of things, each with one job

Until now we kept mixing these. Separated, the whole becomes simple:

| Kind | Words | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Places** (where things live; git repositories today) | **star**, **constellation**, **observatory** | where data is kept and brought together |
| **Ways of seeing** | **lens**, **fulldome** | how data becomes something a person can see and touch |
| **What ocoeco does** | record, **observe**, show | the acts that make it automatic |

## The places: the same shape at three scales

- **A star produces.** It keeps its own data and gathers nothing.
- **A constellation is a family.** Its stars *belong* together: independent, but sharing a purpose. It also keeps data of its own, and this is the part I hadn't seen. The relations between its stars, and the decisions that span them, have had nowhere to live. Today I wrote decisions about ocoeco and oco-agent *together* into whichever star was at hand.
- **An observatory is someone's looking.** It gathers what its owner cares to see. The stars don't belong to it, and needn't even know.

**You're right that star and observatory alone aren't enough. The difference that earns "constellation" its word is *belonging* versus *looking*.** A constellation says something about the stars. An observatory says something about the observer.

## Your first uncertainty: is the fulldome one lens?

**Yes, but a particular one: the outermost.** A lens can be made of lenses. The fulldome is the lens that holds all the others and shows how they connect. That keeps both things you said true at once:
- **It *is* a lens,** made by the same mechanism, with nothing new to invent.
- **It *is* the whole.** What makes it more than a board is the continuity across lenses, and only the outermost lens can show that.

**Every place has the same fulldome,** run over whatever that place holds:
- a star's own data;
- a constellation's stars' data, plus its own;
- an observatory's constellations' data.

That's exactly your phrase: *"the same fulldome backbone, just gathered from multiple stars."*

**So the picture has two symmetries: places nest by gathering, and lenses nest by composing.**

## Your second uncertainty: is there a place for the observer?

**Yes, and you named it: it's the part of ocoeco that gathers.** A constellation gathering its stars, and an observatory gathering constellations or other observatories, are **the same act at different scales**. One part of ocoeco does it all. Today that part is called `harvest` and `discover`, farm and search words in an astronomy family. *Observe* is its natural name.

So ocoeco has three acts:
- **record:** a star producing its data at the hot places, where things are fresh.
- **observe:** gathering from other places.
- **show:** running lenses.

## Something this dissolves

Earlier I worried whether an observatory gathers *data* or *renders*. With your fuller definition of a lens, the tension disappears. If a lens is shared, and anyone in ocoeco can use it, then the same lens over the same data shows the same thing anywhere. **So the observer brings the data and the names of the lenses. Taking a ready render is just a shortcut, not a principle.**

## One caution on the lens

You described a lens as carrying *where it gets its data* as well as *how it shows it*. I agree, with one limit so it doesn't grow into a plugin system. **A lens must declare the data it needs and at least one way to show it.** Bringing its own instruments for producing that data is optional. We prove it by building one.

- **record:** a star producing its data at the hot places, where things are fresh.
- **observe:** gathering from other places.

## Lenses are additive: yes, and it completes the picture

Because ocoeco is a rhizoid, anyone can write a lens, keep it or offer it upstream, and still pull updates, since **a changed lens is a new lens**. That's the same principle that makes the journal safe: you add, you never rewrite. Two small conditions keep it true, and I'll record them with it:
- **A lens may add tables or fields. It never changes what an existing one means.** The shared language is already "a minimum, extra allowed", so this holds today.
- **A lens says which lens it grew from.** Otherwise additive becomes a pile of near-duplicates nobody can choose between. With the lineage recorded, the fulldome can show the family of a lens.

I think you've caught something real. **"Showing" is wrong, and for the reason you give.** A lens doesn't show anything. Light passes *through* it and comes out shaped. The showing happens somewhere else: on the dome.

## What a lens actually does, in its own domain

In optics, a lens is defined by one thing: **it transmits light and brings it to a focus.** A telescope's lens gathers the faint light of a star and focuses it, so that what was a blur becomes something you can make out. The lens adds nothing and displays nothing. It lets the light through, *ordered*.

So the word for a lens's second face is **focus**.

> A lens has two faces: its **glimpse** catches the data, and its **focus** brings it into view.

## Why I think "focus" is right, and what I checked against

- **It's from the domain,** and it's what a lens is *for*.
- **It's plain, and it can be guessed.** "Focus the work lens on this star" needs no manual.
- **It says the true thing about the data:** nothing is created. The same data, brought into focus, becomes legible. That's your whole point about lenses, that the underlying data is the same for everything.
- **It puts the showing where it belongs.** A lens focuses, and what you *see* is on the fulldome. That separation was missing, and "showing" hid it.

**The words I weighed and set aside:**
- **resolve:** the true optics word for telling details apart, but we already say links "resolve", and people "resolve" problems.
- **image:** what a lens forms, but here "image" already means disk and system images.
- **project / projection:** tempting, since a planetarium *projects* onto its dome. But "project" is the very noun we just retired in favour of "star".
- **render:** a graphics word. Honest, but from outside the family.
- **reveal:** plain and lovely, but not optics.

## The whole chain now reads as one physical picture

> A **star** gives off light: its data.
> A **glimpse** catches it, where it's fresh.
> A **lens** lets it through and brings it into **focus**.
> The **fulldome** is where it's seen, as one sky.
> To **observe** is to gather the light of many stars.

So the acts are **glimpse, observe, focus**. I think this also answers where *shine* belongs: it's not an act of ocoeco at all. It's simply what a star does when it works.

Yes, you understood me, and we arrived at the same place: **the projection is the shape that focusing gives the data.** That's not drift. In the code the projection is literally what the act of focusing produces.

I'd asked how a lens should declare "at least one star" or "this total equals that count", and said I couldn't see its form. **Your answer is that those questions were misplaced.** They're about the *data*, and the projection doesn't touch data. - **Is the data sound?** That's the data's business: tad's rules and the relations.
- **Was everything observed?** That's observing's business. The listing cut at 1,000 was this kind.
- **Is the shape sound?** That alone is the projection's.

So there was never a missing "form". I was asking one layer to do another's work.

That also untangles your knot more precisely than my answer did. You said a reliable program needn't watch itself, yet awareness felt necessary. **Both are true, of different layers.** Shape is the program's own, so it can be checked once, in the making, and then needn't be watched. Here is the shape I'd give it. Everything published stays as it is until you've seen this.

## The shape

**1. The contract gains one word: `asked`.**

An input's values are *asked* when they're known only as the program runs, and the program can tell them. That's the only new field. Whether a set is *declared* isn't stored anywhere new. It's read off `allowed`, as today. And a list may now have no `allowed`: its members are then free, or asked.

So the three sources fall out, and **no two fields can disagree**:

| `allowed` | `asked` | The values are |
|---|---|---|
| given | – | **declared**: one of these |
| empty | yes | **asked**: one of whatever exists |
| empty | no | **free**: whatever the type admits |

**2. One question, which is the whole engine: *what fits here?***

Given the words so far, argenv answers with the commands, options and values that can come next, each with its one line. For an asked input it calls the program's own function, **handing it what's already been resolved**. That's the lesson from clap's users, who re-parse the line by hand.

**3. One way to ask from outside: through the environment.** That's argenv's own second door, and nothing is reserved in the program's command space.

**4. Everything else is a surface of that one question:**
- **Tab in a shell:** a few lines per shell, identical for every program.
- **A blank in a form:** your *"being on a blank spot shows what can be entered"*.
- **Help:** the same question asked of an empty line.
- **Man pages and docs:** the contract, laid out.

That's your shape editor's engine, and it means **three hand-written things retire**: snapall's completions, lab-agent's completions, and oco-agent's hand-typed usage text.

## What I'd reject, and why

- **A separate type for open lists** (the issue's second option). A type says what a value *is*. Where it comes from is another matter, and mixing them would double every type.
- **A three-way field stored beside `allowed`.** Two places would say whether a set is closed, they could disagree, and a rule would be needed to keep them honest: a part to carry.
- **Naming a shell command in the declaration,** as `usage` does with `run="…"`. It works for a spec file. In argenv the program is the one that knows, and a string wouldn't be checked by the compiler.

## Left to discovery, as you'd have it

Whether argenv should also *emit* a `usage` spec, as an adapter to that project's generators for more shells and docs. It would cost the core nothing. I'd let friction decide, not decide in advance.

**Recorded, and one fact turned up that makes the trial very small.**

## The fact

argenv's reader, the careful one that understands `--`, short forms, the environment and precedence, **doesn't need its Rust declarations at all.** It reads against plain data:

```
Invocation { args, env }.resolve(model: &[Record]) → Resolution
```

A `Record` is just a key, a type, allowed values, required, a summary. So the cut you described is *already movable inside argenv*. Its typed constants are only one way of producing those records, and **a lens entry can be another**, made as the program runs. There's no build step, no translation to carry, and no new field.

## The trial

**One entry of ocoeco, turned into records, read by argenv's own reader.** If it reads `--title … --status next` and refuses what an entry doesn't have, then:
- ocoeco's own little reader of typed words dissolves into argenv's;
- argenv's reader speaks about lens entries without knowing what a lens is;
- and "a command line is an entry" stops being a sentence and becomes something that runs.

If it *doesn't* fit cleanly, the friction will say exactly what's lacking, and that's worth as much.
